Surah al-Hujurat is Madinan, and its verses number eighteen.

﴿O you who have believed﴾. The opening of the address with the vocative is to alert those addressed to the fact that what falls within its scope is a grave matter, calling for their heightened attention to it, their utmost concern in receiving and observing it. Describing them with faith serves to energise them and to signal that it calls to preserving it and restrains from neglecting it.

﴿Do not put forward﴾: that is, do not perform putting forward, the object being omitted in order to aim at the act itself without regard to its being connected to any particular matter, in the manner of their saying: "So-and-so gives and withholds," meaning he performs giving and withholding. Or it means: do not put forward any matter, the object being omitted in order to generalise it. The first is more fitting to the requirement of the context, since it conveys the prohibition of engaging in the very act, which requires its total absence, and this entails by demonstrative reasoning the absence of its connection to its object. It has also been permitted that "taqdim" means "taqaddum" (advancing), and from it comes "muqaddimat al-jaysh" (the vanguard of the army) for the advanced group. This is supported by the reading of one who recited "lā taqaddamū" by dropping one of the two tā's from "tatqaddamū." It is also read "lā tuqaddimū" from "qudūm" (arrival). His words, exalted is He: ﴿before Allah and His Messenger﴾ are a metaphor taken from what lies between the two directions facing a person's two hands, to disparage what they were forbidden from. The meaning: do not decide a matter before they have judged it. It has been said that the intended meaning is: before the Messenger of Allah; and the mention of Allah, exalted is He, is for His glorification and to signal the sublime station of the Messenger with Him, may He be exalted and glorified. It has been said: it was revealed concerning what took place between Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the appointment of al-Aqra' ibn Habis or al-Qa'qa' ibn Ma'bad.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ in everything you do and refrain from, of sayings and deeds, of which this matter is among the parts.

﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of your sayings.

﴿All-Knowing﴾ of your deeds. Therefore it is His right that He be feared and watched over.

﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾ This begins the prohibition of exceeding bounds in the manner of speaking in the presence of the Prophet, peace be upon him, after the prohibition of exceeding bounds in the speech itself and in the action. The call is repeated, though the earlier address is recent, for emphasis in awakening and alerting, and to indicate that each of the two statements is independent, calling for attention to its matter. That is: do not let your voices go beyond the limit that the voice of the Prophet, peace be upon him, reaches. It is also recited as "لا تَرْفَعُوا بِأصْواتِكُمْ" (do not raise with your voices), taking the بـ (bi, "with") as superfluous.

﴿And do not speak loudly to him﴾ when you address him.

﴿as you speak loudly to one another﴾ That is: a loudness of the kind that is customary among yourselves. Rather, make your voices lower than his voice, peace be upon him, and in addressing him, adopt a gentleness close to a whisper, as is the custom when addressing one who is awe-inspiring and held in honour, and maintain observance of the majesty of prophethood and the greatness of its station. It has been said that the meaning of ﴿And do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another﴾ is: do not say to him, "O Muhammad, O Ahmad," but address him with the title of prophethood. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: When this verse was revealed, Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, I will not speak to you except in a low tone, or like one who speaks in a low tone, until I meet Allah, the Exalted." And it is related from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he would speak to him, peace be upon him, like one who speaks in a low tone, not being heard until he was asked to repeat. And when delegations came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, would send to them someone to teach them how to greet, and would order them to calmness and dignity in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿lest your deeds be nullified﴾ is either a reason for the prohibition, meaning: do not speak loudly out of fear that your deeds will be nullified, or out of dislike that they be nullified, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾. Or it is a reason for the prohibition, meaning: do not speak loudly for the sake of nullification, since loudness, wherever it leads to nullification, is as though it were done for its sake, in the manner of a representation, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿so that it may become for them an enemy and a grief﴾. The intent of what is forbidden, of raising and loudness, is not that which is accompanied by contempt and disrespect, for that is disbelief; rather it is that which is feared to lead to it, from what passes between them in the course of discourse, of raising and loudness, as indicated by His statement, exalted is He: ﴿as you speak loudly to one another﴾ (p-117). Except that raising the voice above his voice, peace be upon him, since it is a clear reprehensible act, was not restricted to anything, nor to what occurs between them in war, or in the disputation of an obstinate opponent, or in intimidating an enemy, or the like.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, who had a deafness in his ear and was loud of voice, and who would sometimes speak to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and be harmed by his voice. And it is related from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that: "When the verse was revealed, Thabit was missing, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, looked for him, and he was informed about his condition. He called him and asked him. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, this verse has been sent down to you, and I am a man of loud voice, and I fear that my deed has been nullified.' The Prophet, peace be upon him, said to him: 'You are not among them. Indeed you will live in goodness and die in goodness, and you are among the people of Paradise.'" As for what is related from al-Hasan, that it was revealed concerning some of the hypocrites who used to raise their voices above his voice, peace be upon him, it has been said: its interpretation is that their prohibition falls under the prohibition of the believers by the indication of the text.

﴿while you do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "tahbata" (be nullified), meaning: while you are not aware of their nullification. In this is additional warning against what they were forbidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 49, verse 3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾ ... etc. It is an encouragement to refrain from what they were forbidden, after a warning against violating it; that is, they lower them out of observance of good manners (adab) or out of fear of opposing the prohibition.

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), in view of its being characterised by what is within the scope of the relative clause (silah), and what it contains of the sense of distance, despite the closeness of the time of the one referred to, because of the magnifying of its status, as has been mentioned many times. It is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿for whom Allah has tested their hearts for piety﴾. That is, He tried them for piety and trained them in it, or He knew them as being for piety and purified for it, since testing is the cause of knowledge. The lam (la) is attached to an omitted element, or to the verb according to the original sense. Or He struck their hearts with various kinds of trials and arduous obligations for the sake of piety, since it does not manifest except through patient endurance in it. Or He purified them for piety, from the verb imtahana al-dhahab (he tested the gold) when he melted it and separated its pure part from its impurity. It is related from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that He removed desires from them.

﴿For them﴾ in the Hereafter.

﴿Is forgiveness﴾ great, for their sins.

﴿And a great reward﴾ whose measure cannot be estimated. The sentence is either another predicate of "inna" like the sentence introduced by the demonstrative, or a resumptive sentence explaining their recompense, praising their condition and implicitly disparaging the bad condition of one who is not like them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 49, verse 4:

﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the private chambers﴾ That is: from outside them, from behind them or in front of them. The "min" (from) here is for the starting point (ibtida'iyyah), indicating that the calling originated from the direction of the back and that the one called was inside the chamber, because the starting point and the endpoint must differ according to direction. This is unlike what would be the case if it were said: "they call out to you behind the chambers." It is also read "al-hujarat" with a fatha on the jim and with a sukun on it, and all three forms are plurals of hujrah. The hujrah is a piece of land enclosed by a wall, and for this reason an enclosure for camels is called a hujrah. It is of the form fu'lah from al-hajr in the sense of maf'ul, like ghurfah and qubdah. What is meant by it is the chambers of the Mothers of the Believers. Their calling out to him from behind them is either because they came to the chambers one by one and called out to him ﷺ from behind them, or because they dispersed among the chambers seeking him ﷺ and called out to him, some from behind this one and some from behind that one, so the action of the parts was attributed to the whole. It has also been allowed that they called out to him from behind the chamber in which he ﷺ was, but it was put in the plural out of reverence for him ﷺ. It has been said: those who called out were 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari and al-Aqra' ibn Habis, who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with seventy men of the Banu Tamim at midday while he was sleeping, and they said: "O Muhammad, come out to us." The calling was attributed to all because they approved of it or ordered it, since it was found among them.

﴿Most of them do not understand﴾ For if they had understanding, they would not have dared to commit such a degree of bad manners.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 49, verse 5:

﴿And if only they had been patient until you came out to them﴾. That is: if their patience and waiting until you came out to them had been realized. Although "anna" (that), together with what follows it in its scope, indicates the verbal noun, it by itself conveys certainty and establishment, owing to the clear difference between your saying "balaghani qiyamuka" (I was informed of your standing) and "balaghani annaka qa'im" (I was informed that you are standing). And "hatta" (until) indicates that patience ought to be limited by his, upon him be blessings and peace, coming out, for it is specific to that which is the endpoint of a thing in itself. For this reason you say "akaltu al-samakata hatta ra'uha" (I ate the fish until its head) and do not say "hatta nisfaha" or "hatta thuluthaha" (until its half or its third). This differs from "ila" (to), which is general. And the phrase "ilayhim" (to them) implies that if he had come out not for their sake, they should have been patient until he addressed them or turned towards them.

﴿Would have been﴾: that is, the aforementioned patience.

﴿better for them﴾ than hastening, because it involves observing good manners and magnifying the Messenger, which warrant praise, reward, and the granting of what they ask for. For it is narrated that they came as a delegation interceding for the captives of Banu al-Anbar, and he released half of them and ransomed the other half.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾: abundant in forgiveness and mercy, vast in both, so He will not constrict the expanse of His forgiveness and mercy for these people if they repent and make amends.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 49, verse 6:

﴿O you who have believed, if a defiantly disobedient person brings you a report, investigate it carefully﴾ That is: "fatabayyanu" means ﴿find out and examine﴾.

It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqba, the half-brother of 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) through his mother, as a collector of alms (musaddiq) to Banu al-Mustaliq, and there was enmity between him and them. When they heard of him, they came out to meet him, and he supposed that they intended to fight him, so he returned and said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "They have apostatized and withheld the zakat." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) resolved to fight them, and then this verse was revealed. It is also said that he sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to them, and he found them calling to prayer and performing the night prayer, and they handed over the charities to him, so he returned. In the ordering of the command to investigate upon the disobedience of the one who reports, there is an indication of the acceptance of the report of a single trustworthy ('adl) narrator in some matters. It is also read as ﴿fatathabbatu﴾, meaning: ﴿hold back until the situation becomes clear to you﴾.

﴿Lest you harm a people in ignorance﴾ Lest you strike ﴿a people﴾ out of caution against ﴿harming them in ignorance﴾, being uncertain of their true condition.

﴿And then become regretful of what you have done﴾ regarding them, after their innocence of what was attributed to them has become evident.

﴿Regretful﴾ grieving a lasting grief, wishing that it had not happened, for the root of these three letters (n-d-m) revolves around persistence.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 49, verse 7:**

﴿Know that among you is the Messenger of God﴾. "Anna" (أنَّ, "that," introducing a clause) with what follows it in its clause fills the place of the two objects of "u'lamu" (اعْلَمُوا, "know"). This takes into account what follows it, the words of God Most High: ﴿If he were to obey you in many matters, you would surely be in distress﴾. The latter clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a clause describing the state of the subject) referring to one of the two pronouns in "fīkum" (فِيكم, "among you"). The meaning is: "Among you is the Messenger of God in a state that you must change, or [you are] in a state..." and that state is that you want him, peace and blessings be upon him, to follow your opinion in many events. Had he done so, you would have fallen into hardship and ruin. This implies that some of them had urged the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to attack the Banu al-Mustaliq, in confirmation of the statement of al-Walid, and that he, peace and blessings be upon him, did not follow their opinion.

As for the use of the present tense (muḍāriʿ), it has been said that it indicates that the avoidance of their distress is due to the avoidance of the continuous obeying of him, peace and blessings be upon him, toward them. Their distress would only result from the continuous obeying of him in whatever matters occur to them, for that would disrupt the affairs of the people (al-ibāla, lit. "the burden," an idiom for the public affairs) and turn the leader into one led. It is not because of obeying him in some matters they see as rare, but rather obeying him would bring them benefit without harm. It has also been said that the present tense indicates that the avoidance of their distress is due to the continuous avoidance of his obeying them in that matter. The negated present tense may indicate the continuation of the negation according to context, as in similar instances of God Most High's words: ﴿nor will they grieve﴾.

The truth is that the continuity indicated by the present-tense form is considered in two ways. In one way, it is considered in relation to what is connected with the verb among temporal matters that renew themselves, namely by considering the continuity in the act itself in an indefinite manner, and then considering the connection of what is linked to it as an explanation of what the continuity pertains to. In the other way, it is considered in relation to the renewing time itself connected to it. This applies when its connection to what it is linked to is considered first, and then its continuity is considered; so it must be understood in terms of time. If by the continuity of obedience is meant its continuity and renewal according to the renewal of its many occurrences, which is made clear by God Most High's words ﴿in many matters﴾, then the correct view is the first, since the basis for avoiding distress is the avoidance of that continuity, whether that avoidance is by the obedience not occurring in any of those many matters at all, or by it not occurring in all of them while occurring in some small part of them. Even if that continuity is not avoided in either of the two ways mentioned, but obedience does occur in some of those many matters at some time, distress would certainly occur. If, however, by it is meant the continuity of obedience occurring in all matters and its renewal according to the renewal and continuity of time, then the correct view is the second. The basis for avoiding distress in that case is not the avoidance of the continuity of the mentioned obedience, since that would necessarily lead to distress; rather, it is the temporal continuity of the avoidance of that obedience occurring in those many matters in one of the two ways mentioned. Even if that avoidance does not continue, such that the obedience occurs at some time, distress would certainly occur.

Know that the more worthy of choice and the more appropriate to consider is the first view, because it better accords with the analogy that requires the avoidance to be applied to the continuity, in the way that "law" (لَوْ, "if") indicating the past is placed before the present-tense form indicating the future. Moreover, considering the continuity as applying to the negation goes against analogy, and it is only resorted to, with the help of context, when it is impossible to proceed according to the requirement of analogy or when there is no additional merit in it, as in God Most High's words ﴿nor will they grieve﴾, where it is understood as the continuous negation of grief from them, since there is no additional benefit in negating the continuity of grief. But when the statement is coherently arranged while observing what analogy requires, deviating from it is an evident contrivance.

As for God Most High's words ﴿But God has made faith beloved to you﴾... this is a turning of the address (tajrīd, a shift of address) and directing it to some of them by way of a corrective addition (istidrāk, a clause that corrects or qualifies what precedes it), clarifying their innocence of the attributes of the earlier people and praising their deeds. That is: "But He, may He be exalted, made faith beloved (مَحْبُوبًا) to you (لَدَيْكم)."

﴿And He adorned it in your hearts﴾, until its love became firmly rooted in them, and for this reason you did what befits it of sayings and deeds.

﴿And made disbelief, wickedness and disobedience hateful to you﴾. For this reason you refrained from what befits them of what has no good in it, of their effects and judgments. Since "love" and "hatred" (in this context) imply the conveying and reaching of love and hatred to them, they are used with the particle "ilā" (إلى, "to").

It has been said that this is a corrective addition explaining the excuse of the earlier people, as if it were said: "What proceeded from you concerning the Banu al-Mustaliq was not a flaw in your creed, but rather from the excess of your love for faith and your hatred for disbelief, wickedness and disobedience." The first view is more apparent, because of God Most High's words ﴿Those are the rightly guided﴾, meaning those who travel the straight path that leads to the truth. The shift to the third person (al-iltifāt ilā al-ghayba, a turn from direct address to third-person reference), as in God Most High's words ﴿And what you give in zakat, seeking the countenance of God, those are the ones who multiply [their reward]﴾, is similar.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 49, verse 8:

﴿As a bounty from Allah and a favor﴾ i.e., and as a blessing. It is a causal clause (ta'lil) for "He made it beloved to you" or "He made it hateful to you," and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad). It has also been said that their accusative form (nasb) is governed by a suppressed verb, i.e., that this occurred as a bounty (fadlan). And it has been said: [it is related to] "they seek a bounty" (yabtaghun fadlan).

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ intensive in knowledge (mubaligh fi al-'ilm), so He knows the states of the believers and the differences in rank among them.

﴿All-Wise﴾ who does everything He does in accordance with the requirement of wisdom (al-hikmah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 49, verse 9:

﴿And if two groups of the believers fight⦆ i.e., they fight one another. The plural is used in view of the meaning.

﴿then make peace between them⦆ by counsel and by calling them to the judgment of Allah the Exalted.

﴿But if one of them transgresses⦆ i.e., oversteps its bounds.

﴿against the other⦆ and is not affected by the counsel.

﴿then fight against the one that transgresses until it returns⦆ i.e., returns.

﴿to the command of Allah⦆ to His judgment, or to what it has been commanded.

﴿Then if it returns⦆ to Him and ceases fighting, out of fear of your fighting.

﴿then make peace between them with justice⦆ by settling what is between them according to the judgment of Allah the Exalted, and do not content yourselves with merely separating them, lest there be fighting between them at another time. The restriction of reconciliation to justice is because injustice is likely to occur after the fighting; and this is emphasised where it is said: ﴿and act justly⦆ i.e., be just in all that you do and all that you leave undone.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly⦆, so He will reward them with the best reward. The verse was revealed concerning a fight that took place between the Aws and the Khazraj during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) with palm stalks and sandals. It indicates that the transgressor does not leave the faith by transgressing, that if he refrains from war he is left alone because he has returned to the command of Allah the Exalted, and that it is obligatory to help the one who has been wronged after offering counsel and striving for reconciliation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 49, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, the believers are but brothers.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming what precedes it, namely the command to reconciliation (islah). That is, they are affiliated to a single origin, which is faith (iman), the thing that necessitates eternal life. The fa' (fa, "so") in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿So make reconciliation between your two brothers⦆ is to signal that the religious bond necessitates reconciliation. Placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, with the attribution to those commanded, is for the sake of emphasizing the obligation of reconciliation and urging it. The singling out of the two for mention is to establish the obligation of reconciliation in what is beyond that by way of priority (al-tariq al-awlawiyya), because strife and corruption multiply in it. It has been said: the intended meaning of "the two brothers" is the Aws and the Khazraj. It is also recited as "bayna ikhwatikum" and "bayna ikhwanikum."

﴿And fear God⦆ in everything you do and everything you leave undone, and among the matters of which the command to reconciliation is part.

﴿That perhaps you may receive mercy⦆, hoping that you will be shown mercy on account of your God-consciousness (taqwa).

O Qur'an, 49:11, in the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim):

﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people﴾, i.e., from among you.

﴿[another] people﴾ also from among you. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿perhaps they may be better than them﴾, is a ta'lil (a stated reason) for the prohibition, or for what it necessitates. That is: perhaps the one being mocked is better in the sight of Allah, exalted is He, than those who mock. The word qawm (people) is specific to men, because they are the qawwamun (those who are in charge) over women. In its origin it is either the plural of qa'im, like sawm and zawr as plurals of sa'im and za'ir, or a verbal noun described by it which became common for the plural. As for its being applied to both groups in expressions like qawm 'Ad and qawm Fir'awn, this is either by taghlib (the masculine taking precedence) or because women are subordinate to them. The choice of the plural is due to the prevalence of mockery occurring in gatherings. The indefiniteness (of qawm) is either for generality, or to intend the prohibition of some of them from mocking others, since it is among what occurs between one another.

﴿nor let women [ridicule] women﴾, i.e., nor let women mock believing women.

﴿[other] women﴾ from among them.

﴿perhaps they may be better than them﴾, i.e., the one being mocked among them.

﴿better than them﴾, i.e., than the women who mock, for the criterion of superiority in both groups is not what appears to people of forms and shapes, nor the conditions and states upon which mockery mostly turns, but rather the matters hidden in the hearts. So no one should dare to belittle another, for perhaps that person is more excellent than him in what Allah, exalted is He, has attached superiority to. Thus he wrongs himself by demeaning one whom Allah, exalted is He, has honored, and by treating lightly one whom Allah, exalted is He, has glorified.

It was also read as ﴿'asaw an yakunu﴾ and ﴿'asayna an yakunna﴾. In that case 'asa (perhaps) is the one that has a predicate (khabar), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fa-hal 'asaytum﴾. As for the first reading, it is the one that has no predicate.

﴿nor defame one another﴾, i.e., let not some of you find fault with others. For the believers are like a single soul. Or: do not do what you find fault with, for whoever does what deserves being found fault with has found fault with himself. Al-lamz is reviling with the tongue. It was also read with a damma on the mim.

﴿nor call one another by nicknames﴾, i.e., let not some of you call others by a derogatory nickname, for al-nabz is, by custom, specific to that.

﴿Wretched is the name of wickedness after faith﴾, i.e., wretched is the remembrance that is raised for believers to be mentioned with wickedness after entering faith, or after being known for it. For the word ism here means remembrance, as in the saying: "his name spread among people for generosity or for baseness." What is meant by it is either the disgracing of attributing disbelief and wickedness to believers, especially since it was narrated that this verse was revealed concerning Safiyya bint Huyayy, who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "The women say to me, 'O Jewess, daughter of two Jews!'" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Why did you not say: 'My father is Harun, my paternal uncle is Musa, and my husband is Muhammad (peace be upon them)'?" Or it indicates that nicknaming is wickedness, and combining it with faith is ugly.

﴿And whoever does not repent﴾ from what he has been forbidden.

﴿then those are the wrongdoers﴾, by placing disobedience in the place of obedience and exposing the self to punishment.

(p-122)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 49, verse 12:

﴿O you who have believed, avoid much of [what may be] assumption.﴾ That is, be on guard against it. The indefiniteness of "much" serves to make obligatory caution and reflection upon every assumption that is entertained, until it is known to which category it belongs. For among assumptions there are some that must be followed, such as assumption regarding practical matters for which there is no decisive proof, and having good assumption of Allah, exalted is He. And among them are some that are forbidden, such as assumption regarding divine matters (al-ilahiyyat) and prophethood (al-nubuwwat) where a decisive proof contradicts it, and evil assumption about the believers. And among them are some that are permitted, such as assumption regarding worldly affairs (al-umur al-ma'ashiyya).

﴿Indeed, some assumption is sin.﴾ This is a justification for the command to avoid, or for what necessitates it, by way of a verifying resumptive clause (al-isti'naf al-tahqiqi). The "ithm" (sin) is the wrongdoing that merits punishment for it. Its hamza is converted from a waw, as if it "yithimu" the deeds, that is, breaks them.

﴿And do not spy׳﴾ That is, do not search for the faults (awrat) of the Muslims. It is of the form tafa''ala from al-jass (probing), because it carries the sense of seeking, just as al-talammus (feeling for) means seeking, since touching carries the sense of seeking. It has come with the meaning of seeking in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And we touched the heaven﴾. It has also been read with the ha' (tahassasu) from al-hass, which is the trace of al-jass and its result; and because the two are close, the senses (al-mashaʿir, al-hawass) are called by both ha' and jim. In a hadith: "Do not pursue the faults of the Muslims, for whoever pursues the faults of the Muslims, Allah will pursue his fault until He exposes him, even within his house."

﴿And let not some of you backbite others.﴾ That is, let not some of you mention others with evil in their absence. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about backbiting (al-ghiba) and he said: "It is that you mention your brother with what he dislikes. If what you said is in him, then you have backbitten him, and if it is not in him, then you have slandered him." And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: backbiting is the relish of the dogs of the people.

﴿Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?﴾ This is an illustration and depiction of what proceeds from the backbiter, in terms of its proceeding from him and its relation to its object, in the most vile and abominable manner, by nature, intellect and law, with exaggerations from various arts. The interrogative is affirmative (istifham taqriri), and the attribution of the verb to "one" (ahad) is a notification that none of the individuals would do that. The attachment of love to what is utmost in hatefulness, the illustration of backbiting by eating human flesh, making the eaten one a brother to the eater and dead, and presenting their likeness as a matter clear and needing no informing, are all present. It has been read "maytan" with shadda (mayyitan), and its accusative is as a state (hal) of "flesh," and it was said: of "brother." The fa' in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so you would detest it﴾ is for the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes of the illustration, as if it was said: since the matter is as mentioned, you have detested it. It has been read "kurrihtumuh," meaning: you have been naturally disposed to detest it.

﴿And fear Allah.﴾ By abandoning what you were commanded to avoid, and regretting what has proceeded from you before.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance and Merciful.﴾ An intensive form regarding the acceptance of repentance and the bestowing of mercy, in that He makes the penitent as one who has not sinned, and He does not restrict that to one penitent over another penitent, but it encompasses all, even if their sins are numerous. It was narrated that "two men among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, sent Salman to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) seeking relish for them, and Usama was in charge of his food, peace be upon him. He said: I have nothing. So Salman informed them, and they said: If we had sent Salman to the well of Sumayha, its water would have dried up. When they returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said to them: What is this I see, the greenness of meat in your mouths? They said: We have not eaten any meat. He, peace be upon him, said: Indeed, you have backbitten." (p-123) And it was revealed.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 49, Verse 13:**

﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female﴾ from Adam and Eve, or We created each one of you from a father and a mother. All are equal in this, so there is no basis for boasting of lineage. It has also been said that this may be an emphasis on the earlier prohibition, by establishing the brotherhood that prevents backbiting (*ightiyab*).

﴿And made you nations and tribes﴾ *Sha'b* (nation) is a great group whose members trace their descent to one origin, and it encompasses the tribes (*qaba'il*). The *qabilah* (tribe) encompasses the *'ama'ir* (clans), the *'imarah* (sub-clan) encompasses the *buton* (branches), the *batn* (branch) encompasses the *afkhadh* (thighs), and the *fakhdh* (thigh) encompasses the *fasa'il* (sub-branches). Thus Khuzayma is a *sha'b*, Kinana is a *qabilah*, Quraysh is an *'imarah*, Qusayy is a *batn*, Hashim is a *fakhdh*, and al-'Abbas is a *fasilah*. It has also been said that the *shu'ub* are the branches of the non-Arabs ('ajam), and the *qaba'il* are the branches of the Arabs.

﴿That you may know one another﴾ That some of you may know others by lineage, so that no one is ascribed to other than his fathers, not so that you may boast of fathers and tribes and claim disparity and superiority in lineage. It is read as *"li-tatarafu"* according to the original form, as *"la-ttarafu"* with assimilation (*idgham*), and as *"li-ta'rifu"*.

﴿Indeed, the most honored of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ This is a justification for the prohibition of boasting in lineages, which is derived from the speech by way of resumptive confirmation (*al-isti'naf al-tahqiqi*), as if it were said: the most honored in His sight, exalted is He, is the most righteous; so if you must boast, then boast in piety. It is also read with the opened *"anna"* by omitting the particle of causation (*lam al-ta'lil*), as if it were said: Why should you not boast of lineages? It is answered: Because the most honored of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you, not the most noble of you in lineage. For the perfection of souls and the differences between persons revolve around piety, so whoever seeks to attain the lofty ranks, let him hold to piety. The Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wishes to be the most honored of people, let him fear Allah." And the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him (ﷺ) said: "O people, people are of two kinds: a believer who is pious and noble before Allah, the Exalted, and a wicked wretch who is contemptible before Allah, the Exalted." It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the nobility of this world is wealth, and the nobility of the Hereafter is piety.

﴿Indeed Allah is Knowing﴾ of you and your deeds.

﴿Acquainted﴾ with the inner states of your affairs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 49, verse 14:

﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed."﴾ It was revealed concerning a group of the Banu Asad who came to Medina in a year of drought. They professed the two testimonies (al-shahadatayn), and they used to say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We have come to you with our belongings and our families, and we did not fight you as the Banu so-and-so fought you," seeking charity and bestowing favor upon him (peace and blessings be upon him) for what they had not done.

﴿Say﴾: as a rejection of them.

﴿"You have not believed"﴾: since faith (iman) is the assent (tasdiq) that accompanies trust (thiqah) and the tranquility of the heart, and this had not come about for you. Otherwise you would not have bestowed favors upon me by what you mentioned, as the end of the surah indicates.

﴿"But say, 'We have submitted'"﴾: for submission (islam) is compliance (infiyad) and entry into peace (silm), and the profession of the testimony and the abandoning of warfare indicate it. The noble arrangement prefers this over saying: "Do not say 'We have believed,' but say 'We have submitted,'" or "You have not believed, but you have submitted," in order to avoid the prohibition against uttering faith, and to avoid presenting their statement as a surrender and an accounting of it, while it is purely a mere claim.

﴿"And faith has not yet entered your hearts."﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in "say"; that is: "But say 'We have submitted' while your hearts are not in agreement with your tongues." The sense of expectation (tawaqqu') contained in "lamma" indicates that these people will have believed afterward.

﴿"And if you obey Allah and His Messenger"﴾ with sincerity and abandoning hypocrisy.

﴿"He will not deprive you of any of your deeds"﴾: He will not diminish them for you.

﴿"Anything"﴾ of their rewards. From "lat yalit layt," meaning he diminished; and it is read "la ya'litkum" from al-alt, which is the dialect of Ghatafan; or "shay'an" from diminution (al-naqs).

﴿"Indeed Allah is Forgiving"﴾ of what has passed from the obedient.

﴿"Merciful"﴾ in bestowing favor upon them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 49, verse 15:

﴿Truly, the believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, and then have not doubted﴾ — they did not become doubtful. "Irtaba" (to doubt, to be in suspicion) is the reflexive form of "raba," used when someone is caused to fall into doubt together with suspicion. In this there is an indication that among them there is something that necessitates the negation of faith from them. And "thumma" (then) here serves to convey that the condition of not doubting in the consideration of faith is not only at the time of its initiation, but also concerns what follows; it is thus like His Exalted saying: "then they remained steadfast" (thumma istaqamu).

﴿And strove with their wealth and their selves in the way of Allah﴾ — in His obedience, across its many kinds of acts of worship: the purely physical, the purely financial, and those that combine both, such as the Hajj and jihad.

﴿Those﴾ — who are described by the fine qualities mentioned.

﴿They are the truthful ones﴾ — that is, those who are truthful in their claim of faith, and no others. It is reported that when this verse was revealed, they came and swore that they were truthful believers, so His Exalted saying was revealed to refute them:

Say: "Will you inform Allah of your religion?" That is: will you tell Him about it by your saying "We have believed"? The expression "teaching" Him about it is used for the sake of severely rebuking them.

﴿And Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the object of "you teach" (tuʿallimūna), emphasizing their rebuke. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And Allah is Knowing of all things﴾, is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) confirming what precedes it; that is, He is thoroughly knowing of all things, among which is what they concealed of disbelief while displaying belief. In this there is further condemnation of their ignorance and a rebuke to them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 49, verse 17:

﴿They consider their Islam a favour upon you.﴾ That is, they count their submission (islam) as a favour (minna) bestowed upon you. And minna is a blessing for which its bestower seeks no reward from the one upon whom it is bestowed. The wordman here carries the sense of qat' (cutting off), because its purpose is to cut off his need. It has also been said: minna refers to a heavy blessing, from the root man.

﴿Say: Do not consider your Islam a favour upon me.﴾ That is, do not count your Islam as a favour to me, or do not bestow (tamunnu) your Islam upon me. The word is in the accusative (fa-nusiba) by the removal of the preposition (bi-naz' al-khafid).

﴿Rather, God bestows a favour upon you, that He has guided you to faith﴾, as you claim, although guidance does not necessarily entail being guided (al-ihtida'). It has also been read as "in hadakum" and "idh hadakum."

﴿If you are truthful﴾ in your claim of faith. Its response is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. That is: then God's favour is upon you. There is in the context of this noble composition a subtlety that is not hidden: for when they named what proceeded from them as faith and bestowed it as a favour, its being faith was negated and it was called submission (islam). It has been said: they bestow favour upon you by what is in reality submission, and it is not worthy of being a favour; rather, even if their claim to faith were valid, the favour belongs to God over them by guiding them to it, not to them.

Indeed, Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth. That is: what is hidden within them.

﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, in your secrets and your openness. How then could what is in your hearts be hidden from Him? It is also read with the letter yā' (i.e., "yaʿmalūn," "they do"). "From the Prophet (ﷺ): «Whoever recites Surat al-Ḥujurāt, he is given a reward equal to the number of those who obeyed Allah and those who disobeyed Him."»
